737.oneliner: One angle-of-attack sensor glitched, so the automation kept pushing the nose down — and the pilots couldn't out-trim it.
737.summary: MCAS trimmed the stabilizer nose-down based on a SINGLE angle-of-attack sensor. A faulty sensor made it fire repeatedly, with more authority than the pilots' counter-trim, re-triggering each time they responded. Certification assumed crews would diagnose it as ordinary runaway trim within seconds; training was minimized to keep a common type rating. Lion Air 610 and Ethiopian 302 were lost. No single broken part explains it: a sensor fault + single-sensor authority + hidden system + training economics + certification assumptions.
737.source: US House T&I Committee Final Report (2020); JATR (2019)

3mi.oneliner: A relief valve stuck open, but the panel light showed it closed — so the operators turned the emergency coolant DOWN. The core uncovered.
3mi.summary: Unit 2 lost coolant through a pressure-operated relief valve (PORV) that stuck open. The operators' only indication was a light wired to the valve's CLOSE command, not its actual position — so their mental model said 'closed'. Rising indications looked like 'too much water' (going solid), the thing they were trained to avoid, so they throttled High-Pressure Injection (emergency coolant). The core uncovered. No operator was incompetent and the valve-stick alone was survivable; the accident was the interaction of a stuck valve, a lying indicator, and correct-by-training operator action.
3mi.source: Kemeny Commission (1979); Perrow, Normal Accidents (1984) ch.1

cf.oneliner: One WAF rule with a catastrophic-backtracking regex was pushed to the whole fleet at once — CPU hit 100% everywhere and much of the web 502'd for ~27 minutes.
cf.summary: A new managed WAF rule contained a regular expression with catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS). It was deployed globally in one step, with no staged/canary rollout and no CPU bound on rule evaluation. On live traffic the regex went exponential, saturating CPU across Cloudflare's edge and returning 502s worldwide. A recent change had moved WAF execution in a way that removed an earlier CPU protection. Recovery came from a global 'WAF kill switch'. No single broken component: a pathological regex + global simultaneous rollout + a removed safeguard.
cf.source: Cloudflare, 'Details of the Cloudflare outage on July 2, 2019' (John Graham-Cumming)
cf.crosslink: A regex/parser pathology — see ../../parser-differentials (ReDoS is a recognizer blowing up on crafted/ordinary input).

S1.label: Safety-I

S1.cite: Hollnagel, 'Safety-I and Safety-II' (2014) — the traditional 'absence of accidents' view, named to contrast with Safety-II

S2.label: Safety-II

S2.author: Erik Hollnagel
S2.cite: Hollnagel, 'Safety-I and Safety-II' (2014); Hollnagel, Wears & Braithwaite, 'From Safety-I to Safety-II: A White Paper' (2015)
